Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Stock Broker
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

Vignette:
Kofi had always been a man who thrived on control and precision, making a successful career for himself as a stock broker in New York City. But that all changed on a typical Monday morning two years ago, when he received the devastating news that his only child, 25-year-old daughter Ama, had died suddenly in a car accident on her way to work. Kofi was consumed by an unbearable grief, and as the days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, he found himself struggling to make sense of the tragedy. As he tried to navigate his new reality without Ama, Kofi became increasingly preoccupied with questions about why this had happened to him. He would spend hours ruminating on every possible explanation, from fate to divine retribution, but no matter how hard he tried, he couldn't shake off the feeling of responsibility that weighed heavily on his shoulders. "What if I had been more involved in her life?" he would ask himself over and over again. In an attempt to cope with these unbearable thoughts, Kofi started to suppress any memories or emotions associated with Ama's passing, trying hard not to think about the trauma. However, this avoidance strategy only seemed to exacerbate his pain. Everyday objects, like the coffee mug Ama had given him for his birthday just a few months before her death, would suddenly bring back vivid memories of their time together, and Kofi would find himself becoming overwhelmed with emotion. He began to avoid anything that reminded him of Ama, including visiting places they used to go to together or even looking at old family photos. As the anniversary of Ama's passing approached, Kofi started to feel an intense sense of restlessness. He began taking more risks in his trading, hoping to prove to himself that he was still capable of controlling the world around him. But this only led to a series of losses, both financial and emotional, as he struggled with feelings of guilt, shame, and fear. "I'm losing everything," he would say to himself, "just like I lost Ama." Kofi also started experiencing flashbacks, where he would suddenly feel as if he was reliving the moment when he received the news about Ama's death. He would find himself in his car, driving home from work, and suddenly be transported back to that fateful day, with all the emotions and memories flooding back. Despite trying hard to remember what happened on the day of Ama's passing, Kofi found it incredibly difficult to piece together a complete picture. Fragments of memories would appear suddenly without warning, only to disappear just as quickly, leaving him feeling frustrated and disoriented. When he tried to deliberately recall the events leading up to her death, he found his mind going blank. As the months went by, Kofi's behavior became increasingly erratic, causing concern among his colleagues and friends. His isolation deepened, and he started to withdraw from social interactions, unable to bear the thought of facing the world without Ama by his side. It was only when Kofi's boss called him into her office, expressing worry about his declining performance and warning him that his job was at risk, that he realized he needed help. As he sat in his therapist's office for the first time, Kofi knew that he couldn't continue living like this – stuck in a cycle of grief, guilt, and avoidance. He hoped that therapy could help him find a way to confront his pain and learn to live with the loss of his beloved daughter Ama. With tears streaming down his face, Kofi whispered, "I just want to be able to remember her without feeling like I'm losing my mind."
